facts.statement: Rhynchaeites is an extinct genus of wading birds whose name means "beak fossil" in Greek.
facts.quote: Rhynchaeites (Greek for "beak fossil") is an extinct genus of wading bird

facts.statement: Rhynchaeites lived in Europe and North America during the Eocene epoch.
facts.quote: which lived in Europe and North America during the Eocene epoch

facts.statement: Rhynchaeites is classified as a stem-group member of the Threskiornithidae family.
facts.quote: a stem-group threshkiornithid, which lived in Europe and North America during the Eocene epoch

facts.statement: Rhynchaeites is one of the oldest known members of the ibis family.
facts.quote: It is one of the oldest members of the ibis family known from fossil remains

facts.statement: The type species Rhynchaeites messelensis is known from many well-preserved fossils found in the Lutetian-aged Messel pit in Germany.
facts.quote: The type species, R. messelensis, is known from many well-preserved specimens from the famous Lutetian-aged Messel pit of Germany

facts.statement: Rhynchaeites was identified as an early ibis in 1983, after previously being thought to be related to painted-snipes or other charadriiforms.
facts.quote: but was identified as an early ibis in 1983

facts.statement: A second species, Rhynchaeites litoralis, was described in 2023 from the Ypresian-aged London Clay of England.
facts.quote: In 2023, a second species, R. litoralis was described from the earlier Ypresian-aged London Clay of England

facts.statement: Rhynchaeites species inhabited different environments, with R. messelensis living in freshwater and R. litoralis in coastal areas.
facts.quote: both species appear to have inhabited different habitats, with R. messelensis inhabiting freshwater habitats and R. litoralis coastal habitats

facts.statement: A third species, Rhynchaeites mcfaddeni, was described in 2026 based on a largely complete specimen from the Green River Formation in the United States.
facts.quote: In 2026, a largely complete, articulated Rhynchaeites specimen from the Green River Formation of the United States was described as the holotype of a third species, R. mcfaddeni

facts.statement: Potential leg bone fossils of Rhynchaeites have been found in the earliest Ypresian Fur Formation in Denmark.
facts.quote: The potential leg bone fossils of Rhynchaeites have also been found in the earliest Ypresian Fur Formation in Denmark

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that the parrot-like fossil Mopsitta tanta might actually be a leg bone belonging to Rhynchaeites.
facts.quote: It has been hypothesized that the supposed parrot relative Mopsitta tanta, known from a single humerus bone, is the same bird as the leg fossils and thus actually belongs in Rhynchaeites too

facts.statement: Rhynchaeites had much shorter legs than modern ibises and lacked sensory nerves in its bill.
facts.quote: Despite its close resemblance to modern ibises, Rhynchaeites differs in several aspects of morphology from them, primarily in its much shorter legs and the apparent lack of any sensory nerves in its bill

facts.statement: Rhynchaeites likely relied on sight to find food rather than the tactile probing used by modern ibises.
facts.quote: The latter suggests that Rhynchaeites primarily relied on sight to find food, as opposed to the tactile probing of modern ibises

facts.statement: Rhynchaeites lived between 56 and 41.03 million years ago during the Ypresian to Lutetian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Lutetian (56 to 41.03 million years ago)

rejected.statement: The short legs of Rhynchaeites are considered a primitive trait, suggesting that long legs evolved multiple times within the Pelecaniformes order.
rejected.quote: The short legs of Rhynchaeites appear to be a plesiomorphic trait, and suggest that long legs evolved multiple times within the Pelecaniformes
